content:
The Quran tells the Prophet to ask forgiveness for his dhanb (47:19) and says that God has forgiven his past and later dhanb (48:2). It rebukes him for frowning at a blind man (80:1-10) and corrects his decisions (9:43; 8:67). A critic asks how a man with "sins" can be the perfect model that 33:21 says he is.[1]

The verses are real, and we list them in full. This article aims to provide context to what Muslim doctrine claims about the protection of prophets, called 'iṣma, insha'Allah, and what it leaves out.

Most Sunni theologians hold that prophets are protected from lying in what they convey, from unbelief, and from major sins. Many allow that a minor slip can occur, and they add that a prophet does not persist in one.[2]

The doctrine is a claim about trustworthiness. The message reached people intact, and the life that carried it was upright. A claim of flawless judgement in every worldly matter belongs to a different doctrine, and Islam does not teach it.[2]

The classical readings of 48:2 vary. Some take the dhanb to be the faults of his community.

Some take it as tark al-awlā, passing over the better of two good courses. Others read it as slips, past and future, forgiven in advance.[3]

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi wrote a whole treatise, 'Ismat al-Anbiya', on verses of this kind. The debate was public and the texts were never hidden.[3]

Every one of these readings keeps the Prophet free of any grave sin.

In 80:1-10 the Prophet turns towards the leaders of Quraysh and away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who had come to learn. In 9:43 he allows the hypocrites to stay behind from a campaign, and the verse opens: "God has pardoned you."[4]

Both are decisions about how to act for the good of the mission. Both are corrected openly, in the text that he himself recited to his followers.[4]

Quran 8:67 corrects the decision taken about the captives of Badr. It concerns a judgement made in a war council, after consultation.[5]

Quran 93:7 says: "Did He not find you ḍāll and guide you?" The commentators read the word as "unaware" of the revelation he had not yet received, in line with 42:52: "You did not know what the Book was, nor faith."[5]

A man who invented his revelations would have left out the passages that correct him. These passages were recited in prayer by the people who watched him every day, and they stand as evidence that the words were not his own.

The Bible records David's adultery and the killing of Uriah (2 Samuel 11), Solomon turning to other gods (1 Kings 11:4-10), Noah's drunkenness (Genesis 9:20-21) and the story of Lot's daughters (Genesis 19:30-36).[6]

Set beside these, a frown at a blind man and a decision about captives are corrections of judgement. The Quran keeps every prophet free of the crimes that the Bible attributes to them.[6]

The Quran never presents the Prophet as more than a man, and it records his corrections in his own voice. Our related articles are do Muslims worship Muhammad? and was Muhammad a narcissist? Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 47:19, 48:2, 80:1-10, 9:43, 8:67, 33:21.
  2. W. Madelung and E. Tyan, "'Iṣma", Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill), vol. 4; Qadi 'Iyad, al-Shifa bi-Ta'rif Huquq al-Mustafa, part 3.
  3. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, 'Ismat al-Anbiya'; al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan (Mecca: Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath, n.d.; vols. 1–16 ed. Mahmud Muhammad Shakir), vol. 22, p. 199, on 48:2, https://shamela.ws/book/43/12835.
  4. Quran 80:1-10, 9:43; al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, vol. 24, p. 217, on 80:1, https://shamela.ws/book/43/14132, and vol. 14, p. 272, on 9:43, https://shamela.ws/book/43/7840; ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, ed. Sami ibn Muhammad Salama (Riyadh: Dar Tayba, 1999), vol. 8, p. 319, on 80:1, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/4365, and vol. 4, p. 158, on 9:43, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/1957.
  5. Quran 8:67, 93:7, 42:52; al-Tabari on 93:7; the Arabic texts are on altafsir.com.
  6. 2 Samuel 11-12; 1 Kings 11:1-10; Genesis 9:20-21, 19:30-36.
